name: Hay's Russet
lede: Hay's Russet is a dark, reddish orange-brown from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary, over-represented in paintings from Tibet and carried under a different name in Japan's own color lists.

sections.title: One name in two systems
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 “Color Standards and Color Nomenclature” lists Hay's Russet at hex #92513E among the names he credits to a person [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[brownish-orange]], [[deep-orange-coloured-brown]] and [[polished-brown]], at 3.7, 3.7 and 3.8 ΔE [1]. The 1955 Inter-Society Color Council catalog repeats the name in the block it calls dark reddish orange [1]. Our Japanese traditional-color list carries the same hue as *Sōdenkaracha* (宗傳唐茶), meaning a faded, spicy red-brown, a separate naming line that reaches the same color by its own route [3].

Its nearest neighbor in our color graph is [[brownish-orange|Brownish Orange]], only 3.7 units away and more vivid [1]. Against the basic color words it reads closest to [[sienna|Sienna]], 6.2 units off [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive matches this color in 3.69% of 23,781 paintings, 877 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 564 [2]. That makes it more common than 84% of the named colors in our set [2]. Unusually, it peaks early rather than late: 10.6% of the 142 paintings we have from the 1200s carry it, 2.5 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 74% of its 564 appearances [2]. John Singer Sargent holds it in 9 of 287 works here, and the color is sharply over-represented in Tibet, 8.1 times the expected rate [2]. Our earliest match dates to the year 1100, 812 years before Ridgway's 1912 book recorded the name, a floor rather than a first, since a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment [2].
